summary: Lists requirements for the TCP/IP header compression scheme to be developed by the Robust Header Compression working group. It discusses scope, performance, assumptions about the environment, and intellectual-property concerns. Its structure comes from RFC 3096. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Packet labels can be long and repeat themselves. This memo lists what a good way of shortening those labels needs to do, before anyone designs it.

questions: why compress tcp headers on cellular links
subtitle: The checklist a TCP/IP header compression scheme for ROHC had to meet before it was designed.

tldr.problem: Existing TCP header compression was not robust over links with high error rates and long round-trip times, such as cellular links, and did not handle modern TCP features well.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists requirements in five groups: impact on Internet infrastructure, supported headers and TCP streams, performance, link-layer characteristics, and intellectual property.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document only. It specifies no compression scheme itself, and a protocol meeting it would need its own IANA assignments.

today: RFC 4163 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It states requirements only and defines no protocol, so it adds no security risks by itself.

sections.title: Goals of ROHC for TCP
sections.content:
The RObust Header Compression (ROHC) working group develops header compression schemes that perform well over links with high error rates and long link round-trip times, such as W-CDMA, EDGE and CDMA2000 cellular links. Its main objective had been IP/UDP/RTP, defined by requirements in RFC 3096, and this document inherits that structure.

Earlier TCP schemes (RFC 1144 and RFC 2507) ran mostly over reliable links. TCP header compression will now be used over less reliable links, so robustness matters, along with better efficiency, compression of TCP options, and fitting into the ROHC framework (RFC 3095).
sections.eli5: Phones talk over shaky radio links where messages get lost. Shortening packet labels there is harder, so the group wrote down what a TCP shortener must handle.

sections.title: Infrastructure and Header Requirements
sections.content:
Transparency: a header that is compressed and then decompressed must be semantically identical to the original, or the packet must be discarded. Ubiquity: the scheme must not require changes to existing IP (v4 or v6) or TCP implementations, and must work for all expected TCP variants.

On supported headers, the scheme must support IPv4 and IPv6 (including IPv6 extension headers and ECN bits), Mobile IP headers, and arbitrary TCP streams. It should compress headers with IPSEC subheaders where NULL encryption is used, although the encrypted part of an ESP header and the cryptographic data in an AH header cannot be compressed.

Packets with any TCP option must be compressible, even if the option itself is not. SACK and Timestamp are the options that should get their own compression.
sections.eli5: The shortened label must expand back to exactly the same label, and the shortener must work with the computers already out there without changing them.

sections.title: Performance Requirements
sections.content:
The scheme must give low relative overhead, with compression efficiency better than RFC 2507 under equivalent conditions. Losses between compressor and decompressor should not cause further packet losses or damage the context so that later headers decompress wrongly.

The TCP checksum must be carried unmodified in all compressed headers, so the scheme does not interfere with TCP's end-to-end error detection. The scheme should also compress short-lived transfers efficiently, minimizing context initiation headers.

On misordering, the scheme should efficiently handle moderate misordering (2-3 packets) and must correctly handle packet misordering in general. It should not add significantly to the system delay budget.
sections.eli5: The shortener should save space, keep working when some packets vanish, cope with packets arriving out of order, and not slow things down.

sections.title: Link Layer and IPR Requirements
sections.content:
The scheme must be implementable, possibly less efficiently, without explicit feedback from decompressor to compressor, because some links have no feedback channel. It must operate under all expected link delay conditions and fit into the ROHC framework with other profiles. Over tunnels, misordering between compressor and decompressor often cannot be avoided, so the scheme should not prohibit it.

The working group must also work to gain a high degree of confidence that no known intellectual property claims cover the final solution. The RFC argues that only unencumbered solutions, or ones whose terms impose no hindrance on implementation and deployment, are acceptable to the Internet at large.
sections.eli5: It must work even when the receiver cannot talk back, and it must not be tied up by patent claims that stop people from using it.
